name: Radiating Star in de Sitter Space
description: A spherical source of null radiation in a spacetime with a positive cosmological constant.
convention: We work in units with $G = c = 1$. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: A radiating spherical body sits in a universe with a positive cosmological constant. In outgoing null coordinates its spacetime has the line element $ds^2=-\left(1-2m(u)/r-\Lambda r^2/3\right)du^2-2\,du\,dr+r^2d\Omega^2$, where $u$ is retarded time, $r$ is the areal radius, and $m(u)$ is the mass in units of length [campos2025cosmological, vick1985vaidya]. Ronald L. Mallett presented an exact solution for a radiating body in a de Sitter background in 1985 [campos2025cosmological, mallett1985radiating]. Mallett wrote the line element in diagonal coordinates, with a mass that depends on both time and radius [campos2025dynamical]. D. Vick presented the exterior of a radiating star in a de Sitter universe in retarded coordinates later that year [vick1985vaidya].¶The radiation travels along outgoing null surfaces $u=\mathrm{constant}$. The outgoing energy density is nonnegative when $m'(u)\leq 0$, and the mass is nonincreasing [campos2025cosmological]. The mass falls as outgoing radiation carries energy away, with $8\pi T_{uu}=-2m'(u)/r^2$ in units $G=c=1$ [campos2025cosmological].¶The same family admits an ingoing null description with advanced time $v$ and mass $m(v)$ [senovilla2023ultramassive]. When $m'(v)\geq 0$, the incoming null radiation satisfies the dominant energy condition and the mass is nondecreasing [senovilla2023ultramassive]. A decreasing mass in advanced time describes an inward flux of negative energy, a model used for evaporation near a black hole [mbonye1999horizons].¶Mallett studied an evaporating black hole during inflation in 1986, following its apparent and event horizons [mbonye1999horizons, mallett1986erratum, mallett1986evolution]. Mallett related the Hawking temperature of the apparent horizon to the critical temperature of grand unification and found a radiation rate slightly below that of ordinary evaporation [mallett1986evolution]. Later that year Mallett estimated the backreaction from the stress tensor of a massless scalar field in two dimensions [mallett1986back]. Jerzy Matyjasek built an evaporating black hole on this geometry in 1987 and evaluated the incoming part of the stress tensor and its effect on the evaporation [matyjasek1987cosmological].¶Alberto Patino and Hector Rago presented an exact solution for a radiating charged particle in a de Sitter universe in 1987 [patino1987radiating]. Mallett gave the metric of a rotating, radiating, charged mass in a de Sitter space the following year [mallett1988metric]. Kristine M. Larsen and Mallett derived the motion of false vacuum bubbles in these geometries in 1991 and found that it differs from the motion in the Schwarzschild-de Sitter geometry [larsen1991radiation]. The luminosity an outside observer measures departs from the Hawking value, a signature of a child universe [larsen1991radiation].¶Wung-Hong Huang computed the stress tensor of a massless scalar field on this geometry in two dimensions in 1992 and found that inflation slows the evaporation and that the backreaction speeds it once $\Lambda$ is large enough [huang1992hawking]. The outgoing flux diverges on the Cauchy horizon, where the curvature stays finite, so the classical geometry cannot carry the evaporation consistently [huang1992hawking]. Brian D. Koberlein and Mallett argued that the limits Huang took are unphysical [koberlein1994comment]. Koberlein and Mallett found that inflation allows supermaximal charged black holes, and with them primordial naked singularities [koberlein1994charged]. Koberlein found in 1995 that the cosmological constant couples to the angular momentum of a rotating charged black hole and deforms its event horizons, leaving quasinaked singularities visible from the equator and hidden from the poles [koberlein1995rotating].¶Zheng Zhao and coauthors located the event horizons of the black hole and of the universe in 1994 from the Klein-Gordon and Dirac equations near those horizons, together with their Hawking temperatures [zhao1994hawking]. Feng He, Zhao, and Sung-Won Kim found in 2001 that the entropy of a scalar field in thin layers near the two horizons is a linear sum of their areas [he2001statistical]. Jun Ren and Zhao treated the emission as tunnelling across the event horizon in 2006 and found a leading correction to the semiclassical emission rate [ren2006tunnelling].¶S. M. Wagh and Sunil D. Maharaj sent radiation into empty de Sitter space in 1999 with a mass growing linearly in advanced time ($2m=\lambda v$), and found a locally naked central singularity for $\lambda\leq 1/8$, the same condition as without $\Lambda$ [wagh1999naked]. With $\Lambda$ this geometry has no proper conformal Killing symmetry, and asymptotic flatness plays no part in forming the naked singularity [wagh1999naked]. Sushant G. Ghosh and Aroonkumar Beesham showed in 2000 that these shell focusing singularities are strong curvature singularities and scalar polynomial ones [ghosh2000strong].¶Fred C. Adams, Manasse R. Mbonye, and Gregory Laughlin conjectured in 1999 a luminosity of the form Mallett had used [adams1999possible]. On that conjecture, black holes heavier than about $4\times10^{24}$ g absorb vacuum energy and grow until their apparent horizons vanish [adams1999possible]. Mbonye extended the horizon analysis of Mallett to higher dimensions that year, following the apparent and event horizons of the black hole and the cosmological region for negative ingoing energy [mbonye1999horizons]. Neal Dalal and Kim Griest computed the flux into the black hole horizon in 2000 and found that the black hole absorbs only the Gibbons-Hawking radiation of the cosmological horizon, so all known black holes evaporate [dalal2000black]. They argued that the luminosity Mallett used in 1986 is in error [dalal2000black].¶In the ingoing description, the apparent horizons lie at the positive roots of $1-2m(v)/r-\Lambda r^2/3=0$ [mbonye1999horizons]. For $0<9\Lambda m^2<1$ there are two such radii, associated with the black hole and the cosmological region [senovilla2023ultramassive]. The event horizons depend on the global evolution and need not coincide with those instantaneous radii [senovilla2023ultramassive, mbonye1999horizons]. Jiří Podolský and Otakar Svítek showed in 2005 that Robinson-Trautman spacetimes containing pure radiation and a cosmological constant exist for any smooth initial data and approach this spherically symmetric geometry [podolsky2005]. Alberto Saa wrote the geometry in double null coordinates in 2007, in any dimension above two, and found that a black hole evaporating by the Stefan-Boltzmann law leaves a naked singularity behind a Cauchy horizon [saa2007ndimensional].¶Abhay Ashtekar, Béatrice Bonga, and Aruna Kesavan took null dust collapsing into empty de Sitter space as their simplest dynamical example of an asymptotically de Sitter spacetime in 2015 [ashtekar2015asymptotics]. The energy charge at past infinity grows with the inflowing flux and equals the final mass once the flow stops, and the cosmological event horizon separates from the Killing horizon of the final Schwarzschild-de Sitter region [ashtekar2015asymptotics]. Akash K. Mishra, Sumanta Chakraborty, and Sudipta Sarkar found in 2019 that while the mass grows the photon sphere depends on $\Lambda$; at constant mass it sits at $r=3m$ for every $\Lambda$ [mishra2019understanding].¶José M. M. Senovilla studied incoming radiation that builds up the mass of a black hole in a de Sitter background [senovilla2023ultramassive]. In that model, the two marginally trapped tubes meet when $9\Lambda m^2=1$. If the incoming mass rises beyond this threshold, the resulting spacetime has a future singularity reached by every observer in the model [senovilla2023ultramassive]. Future null infinity and the event horizon then cease to exist, and the round sphere where the tubes meet has the largest area a stable marginally trapped surface can have, $4\pi/\Lambda$ [senovilla2023ultramassive]. Senovilla showed in 2023 that this behaviour is generic: when stable marginally trapped surfaces approach that area, a marginally trapped tube changes signature at a round sphere of Gaussian curvature $\Lambda$, and a future singularity follows [senovilla2023beyond].¶Thiago de Lima Campos, Carlos Molina, and José Ademir Sales Lima studied the mass loss as seen by cosmological observers [campos2025cosmological]. They followed a family of observers constructed from curves that comove in de Sitter space. In their evaporation model, some of these observers see a nonzero mass even as their cosmological time tends to infinity [campos2025cosmological]. Valentin Boyanov, Luis J. Garay, Alberto García Martín-Caro, and Gerardo García-Moreno found in 2026 that Hawking radiation from a slowly accreting black hole shrinks its horizon and pushes the cosmological horizon outward [boyanov2026semiclassical]. Evaporation can return part of a spacetime headed past the critical mass to below it, so that future null infinity survives in one region and the future singularity in another [boyanov2026semiclassical].

related.text: A constant mass in a universe with a positive cosmological constant. With $m$ constant, the radiation vanishes.
The background with $m=0$, a universe with a positive cosmological constant.
A spherical radiating body with charge and no cosmological constant. Its mass and charge can vary with retarded time [bonnor1970].

coordinates.name: Outgoing Eddington-Finkelstein

parameters.description: Mass as a function of null time, measured as a length

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(u, r, \theta, \phi)$, with the retarded null coordinate $u$ a length and $r$ the areal radius. The mass $m(u)$ is a function of $u$ alone. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

coordinates.name: Ingoing Eddington-Finkelstein

parameters.description: Mass as a function of null time, measured as a length

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(v, r, \theta, \phi)$, with the advanced null coordinate $v$ a length and $r$ the areal radius. The mass $m(v)$ is a function of $v$ alone. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.
